>Here is a rule of thumb for the identification of surrogate activities.
>  Given a person who devotes much time and energy to the pursuit of goal X,
>  ask yourself this: If he had to devote most of his time and energy to
>  satisfying his biological needs, and if that effort required him to use his
>  physical and MENTAL FACULTIES in a VARIED and INTERESTING  way, would he
>  feel SERIOUSLY DEPRIVED because he did not attain goal X?
>  If the answer is no, then the person's pursuit of goal X is a surrogate
activity.

It follows that if the answer is yes, then it is not a surrogate activity, and
therefore worthwhile.

The caps above are mine, because I find this to be a most intriguing part of
this argument. TK does recognize the need for mental stimulation, not just
physical, in making a living. 

I think that the part on surrogate activities is a call for people to look at
what they really have to offer, and really would be happiest at doing, not
holding themselves to the limited choices of the growth/production based
society. Society undervalues certain talents and overvalues others; people
therefore pursue those fields that are valued, no matter their natural
inclination. A truly free society would allow people to follow their dreams,
instead of pursuing surrogate activities. 

Utopia, of course, correctly translates as nowhere. Yet the free society ideal
is worth pursuing. Some parts of this ideal might be accomodated.

I think that this was a call for creativity of the spirit, and for
diversification, things we lose as we become evermore a homogenous global
society.

I truly wish that TK will elaborate on this passage.

And, thank you John for the manifesto postings!

-Susan
